Thereafter, petitioner was taken to Ram Lal Kundan Lal Orthpedic Hospital, Pandav Nagar, Delhi.

sentences.text: 3. All of the respondents put in their appearance and copy of DAR alongwith documents were supplied to them.

3.1. In his separate written statement filed by respondent No.1, it is mentioned that respodent No.1 is neither the driver nor the owner of the offending vehicle and he has been falsely been implicated by the owner of the motorcycle in connivance with the police and injured.
It is further stated that present claim petition is not maintainable in the present form.
He further stated that the accident, if any, has happened solely because of the negligence of the petitioner.

It is further mentioned that story of owner regarding missing of motorcycle is false as there was no report on 26.08.2017 of missing of motorcycle and the report was lodged after 4 days of the accident.
3.2 Respondent No.2/owner has filed his separate written statement.

In his written statement, he mentioned that petitioner has no right to get any compensation from the owner, as the vehicle has already been stolen on 26.08.2017 and in this regard he lodged an e-FIR bearing No. 026333 dated 30.08.2017 PS Gandhi Nagar.
He further mentioned that petitioner, with collusion of police, falsely implicated the vehicle of respondent to get compensation.
The vehicle of R-2 bearing registration No. DL-8SBJ-0275 is duly insured with the respondent No. 3 / insurer.

3.3. R3/Insurer has filed its separate writen statement taking plea that respondent No.1 was not holding any valid driving licence on the date of accident and thus no liability can be fastened on respondent No.3.

Other general defenses have been taken by R3.
4.
On the basis of the pleadings of the parties, following issues were framed on 05.02.2018:-

( i) Whether Mr. Anand Varshney sustained injuries in a motor vehicular accident happened on 26.08.2017 at about 12:45 pm at U- Block, Opposite Wine shop, U-60,
Shakarpur, Delhi, within jurisdiction of PS Shakarpur, due to rash and negligent driving of motorcycle bearing Registration No.DL-8SBL-0275 (motor-cycle) being driven by Respondent No.1 / Tahir?

(OPP)

(OPR1 & R2)

(iv) Whether the petitioner is entitled to interest on the award amount, if so, at what rate of interest and for which period?

8. The issues are decided as follows- 9.
In an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and in fact is the preponderance of probabilities which is applied in civil cases.
It is also the law that the tribunal is not bound by the technical rules of evidence.
Further in holding any inquiry under section 168, The Claims Tribunal may follow such summary procedure as it thinks fit.
10. Now in this case, the petitioner Anand Varshney is injured and witness of the accident.
In order to establish his claim, he has examined himself as PW-2.
He stated on oath in the affidavit about the accident and how it was caused.

He has clearly deposed that on 26.08.2017 at about 12:45 pm, he was going from Laxmi Nagar Metro Station to his office located at S-561, School Block, Shakarpur,
Delhi and when he reached at U Block, Bus stop near wine shop, a motorcycle bearing registration No. DL-8SBL-0275, came from wrong side at a very high speed and being driven in a rash and negligent manner and hit the petitioner with great force.

He further deposed that as a result of this,
he fell down on the road and sustained fracture on his right lower tibia distal 1/3rd and various other injuires all over his body.
Thereafter, he was shifted to Ram Lal Kundan Lal Orthopedics Hospital, by PCR van and remained hospilized there from 26.08.2017 to 28.08.2017.

sentences.text: If any party does not accept such charge-sheet, the burden must be on such party to adduce evidence.

If the Tribunal feels that charge-sheet is collusive, it can record that charge-sheet cannot be accepted and call upon the parties at any stage to adduce oral evidence of accident and alleged negligence.
In such cases, issue of negligence must be decided on other evidence ignoring the charge-sheet.
No evidence was led by any of the respondents in their defence and R1 did not enter into witness box to assail the claim of the petitioner.
13. Respondent no.1 and 2 the driver and owner of the offending vehicle, did not lead any evidence to prove anything contrary to the claim of the petitioner.

In the case of Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Cmpany Ltd vs Smt. Kamlesh and Others2009 (3) AD Delhi 310 it was held that an adverse inference can be drawn when the driver of the offending vehicle does not enter into the witness box.

sentences.text: Even the insurance company has not led any evidence to disprove the claim of the petitioner.
Though R-2 / registered owner has taken up the plea that his vehicle was stolen prior to the date of accident, he has not led any evidence in support of this defence / plea.

It is seen that in reply to the notice under section 133 of M.V. Act, R-2 had replied to the police that on 26.08.2017,
he had parked his motor-cycle in Gandhi Nagar Market at 9.15 am and when he came out at 10:45 am, his motor-cycle was not found.

He also provided copy of e-FIR bearing No. 026333/17 to the police and both of these documents i.e. copy of notice under section 133 of M.V. Act and copy of the said FIR are part of charge-sheet attached to the DAR.
However, there is not a whisper in the charge-sheet to show that any investigation was conducted by the police to conclude that the offending vehicle was indeed stolen on 26.08.2017.

A perusal of the e-FIR shows that the FIR was lodged on 30.08.2017, whereas the accident is stated to have taken place on 26.08.2017 at 12:45 pm and theft is stated to have occurred on the same day, prior to accident.
There is no explanation from R-2 as to why no complaint was given to the police on 26.08.2017 itself.

No evidence has been led by R-2 which could even prima facie suggest that his vehicle was stolen from Gandhi Nagar Market or that the same was never handed over to R-1 / Tahir by R-2 Himanshu Goswami.
No CCTV footage of Gandhi Nagar Market was proved and placed on record.
Hence, I find no merit in the plea regarding offending vehicle being stolen, as taken by R-2 in his written statement.

ISSUE No.2:
15.
The onus to prove this issue was on the respodents No.1 and 2.

ISSUE No.3:
16.
Section 168 of the Act enjoins the Claims Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and reasonable.
The compensation should not be a windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.
17. The case of Raj Kumar vs Ajay Kumar & Another (2011) 1 SCC 343, is one of the most prominent judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court which deals with compensation in injuries cases.

entities.text: Raj Kumar vs Ajay Kumar & Another (2011) 1 SCC 343
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was held in this case that in routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under the heads-(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation, nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured ,
comprising (a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment and (iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.

Where the claimant suffers a permanent disability as a result of injuries, the assessment of compensation is also to be done under the head of loss of future earnings which would depend the effect and impact of such permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured.
The tribunal should not mechanically apply the percentage of permanent disability as the percentage of economic loss or loss of earning capacity.

What requires to be assessed by the tribunal is the effect of the permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured after assessing the loss of earning capacity in terms of percentage of the income.
It has to be quantified in terms of money to arrive at the future loss of earnings by applying standard multiplier method.
All injuries or permanent disabilities arising from injuries do not result in loss of earning capacity.

If there is no loss of employment or earning capacity, there may not be any need to award any compensation under the head of loss of future earnings, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities in consequent to his injuries.

sentences.text: During his examination-in-chief, PW2 deposed that he had engaged an attendant but no evidence was led in this regard.

During his cross-examination, for the first time, he disclosed the name of his attendant as 'Suresh Kumar' but he also testified that he did not take any receipt from the attendant Suresh Kumar and did not even know his address.
No photograph, parentage, contact number and details of Suresh Kumar is filed.
PW2 deposed that he was not aware whether Suresh Kumar had any special training or diploma to give attendant service.
According to PW2, he appointed Suresh Kumar after coming to know about his particuclars through placement agency.
However, in the very next line, PW2 stated that "I did not inform the agency about employemnt of Suresh Kumar as attendant".
According to PW2, Suresh Kumar worked for him for 5 months and was paid in cash.
Neither any bank document is filed and proved on record to suggest withdrawal of Rs.10,000/- per month and payment to Suresh Kumar as claimed nor details of any placement agency is filed on record.

It is further relevant to mention that Suresh Kumar is not named in the evidence by way of affidavit of PW2 and was not even examined before the Tribunal as a witness to prove the tall claim of PW2 regarding hiring his services and payment.

Though no cogent evidence has been led to show that petitioner had hired any attendant during his treatment, it cannot be ignored that family members of petitioner might have had to render their services for providing assistance to the petitioner for his routine activities and that would definitely suffer their work/job.

For claiming compensation, necessity of employing a professional attendant/ care taker is not required and the petitioner should be compensated for the value of services of the family members,
which has been or would be necessitated by the wrong doing of the driver.

(DTC & Ors Vs. Lalita,
1983 ACJ 253).
Therefore, the petitioner is awarded a sum of Rs.10,000/- as attendant charges.
24. Thus, petitioner is granted a total compensation of Rs.30,000/- (20,000+10,000) under this head.

LOSS OF INCOME DURING TREATMENT :-
25.
Petitioner deposed that at the time of accident, he was self employed and running business of online electrial goods and earning about Rs.27,000/- per month.
He has also proved on record his academic documents i.e. Marksheet B.Sc part I and part II examination result, showing that he passed those examinations.
He has also filed on record his Income Tax Returns for the assessement year 2016-17, showing his gross total income as Rs.3,23,507/-.
This income tax returns was filed on 25.03.2017.

Even though petitioner has not produced any document in support of his self employment and earning, other than this ITR and no other ITR has been filed and proved on record,
in my considered view, this ITR for the relevant period cannot be ignored.
Hence, it can be safely assumed that petitioner was earning about Rs.26,000/- per month.

Petitioner has not lead any evidence to show that he was suggested bed rest for any particular period of time and he was advised not to do his online business for any given number of days or months, solely on account of injuires sustained in the accident.

Considering the nature of injuries as reflected through treatment papers of Ram Lal Kundan Lal Orthopaedics Hospital and testimony of petitioner, it can be fairly assumed that the petitioner would not have been able to continue daily affairs in usual manner and must have remained incapacitated to work for about 2 months.

sentences.text: LOSS OF FUTURE INCOME ON ACCOUNT OF PERMANENT DISABILITY :
26. Petitioner has deposed that he suffered permanent disability to the extent of 13% in relation to left lower limb.
PW3 Dr. Sanjeev Gambhir has proved the disability certificate Ex.PW3/1 as well as assessment sheet Ex. PW3/2.
He deposed that except the discharge summary issued by Ram Lal Kundan Lal Hospital, no other medical document was shown / provided by the petitioner regarding his treatment.
Further, no physiotherpy record was shown by the petitioner.
He also deposed that "It is correct that if the patient had undergone any phyisotherepy , the diability could have been reduced".

Coming to the testimony of PW2, he has not specified in his evidence as to what kind of problem he is facing in his busines of online selling of electrial goods on account of the permanent disability in question.

Even though he deposed in his testimony attested on 01.02.2018 that post accident, he substantially lost, his complete income and he is not able to continue his work till date,
there is no explanation by him as to in what manner he was disabled to work completely on account of permanent disability of mere 13% and how does this permanent disability translate to any functional disability in his day-to-day workspace.
27. During his examination in-chief, PW2 stated that he was self- employed and running business of online electrial goods.
There is nothing in his testimony to show that PW2 was running his online business from any office or whether work place was within confines of home.
He has not filed on record any document regarding any sale and purchase of any electrial goods.
Apart from his oral assertion, petitioner has not produced any document to show that he was running any sort of business from anywhere.
No bill book, tax invoice etc have been placed or proved on record to show that petitioner was self-employed and doing any business.
Petitioner has not explained as to in what manner he shall not be able to work as per his ability and qualification on account of permanent disability suffered by him.

Petitioner has not led any evidence to show what exact work he was doing prior to accident and for how many hours, to arrive at any conclusion that petitioner is not able to work as before, to his detriment and that it is due to accident solely.
Hence, petitioner is not entitled to any compensation under this head.

ISSUE NO. 4 (INTEREST):
31.
Petitioner has pursued his case since the year 2017.

Therefore, he is entitled for interest @ 7.5%
per annum on the aforesaid award amount from the date of filing of the petition till realization.
Howevear, a careful future of the case file reflects that vide order dated 06.01.2020, it was observed that petitioner would not be entitled for interest from 08.08.2019 till conclusion of evidence.
The PE was concluded by petitioner on 16.01.2023.
The interest on the award amount, if any, shall not be payable to the petitioner from 08.08.2019 till 16.01.2023.
However, record further shows that from 04.04.2020 till 27.07.2021, no effective hearing could be given by the Tribunal on account of Corona Pandemic and futher absence of Ld. Presiding Officer.
Hence, I consider it proper to modify the said order to the extent that interest on award amount, if any, for the period from 04.04.2020 till 27.07.2021 shall be payable to the petitioner.
32. Thus, this issue is decided in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents.

LIABILITY:
33.
Now, the question arises as to which of the respondents is liable to pay the compensation amount.
As insurance company has contractual and statutory liability to indemnify the insured, the Insurance company is liable to compensate the third party.

However, it is the admitted case that respodent No. 1 did not have valid and effective driving licence on the date of accident and on this aspect issue No.2 has already been decided against R-1 and R-2.
However, the breach in question is not such as would affect the right of third party, once it is established that vehicle was covered under the policy of insurance.
Law is well settled that insurance company would be entitled for recovery of the compensation amount from the driver and registered owner /insured of the offending vehicle.

In case titled as Gurmeet Singh vs. The New India Assurance Co. Ltd & Ors, MAC App 288/2021 decided on 06.10.2023, it has been held that the respondent no. 3 / insure is entitled to recover the compensation amount paid to the claimants.

opennyai_summary.issue:

Shakarpur, Delhi, within jurisdiction of PS Shakarpur, due to rash and negligent driving of motorcycle bearing Registration No.DL-8SBL-0275 (motor-cycle) being driven by Respondent No.1 / Tahir?
(OPP) 
(ii) Whether the respondent No.1 / driver was holding a valid and effective driving licence to drive the motor-cycle bearing registration No. DL-8SBL- 0275 at the time of accident?
(OPR1 & R2)
(iii) Whether the petitioner is entitled to compensation, if so, to what amount and from whom?
(iv) Whether the petitioner is entitled to interest on the award amount, if so, at what rate of interest and for which period?
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and in fact is the preponderance of probabilities which is applied in civil cases.
It is also the law that the tribunal is not bound by the technical rules of evidence.
Further in holding any inquiry under section 168, The Claims Tribunal may follow such summary procedure as it thinks fit.
(New India Assurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Washeema Bano (2022) SCC OnLine All 403 and Mangla Ram vs Oriental Insurance Company Ltd (2018) 5SCC 656).
12. In New India Assurance Company Ltd vs Pazhaniammal (2011) (2) KLT 648, the Hon'ble High Court of Kerala has held that as a general rule, it can be accepted that production of charge-sheet is prima facie sufficient evidence of negligence for the purpose of claim under section 166 MV Act.
If any party does not accept such charge-sheet, the burden must be on such party to adduce evidence.
If the Tribunal feels that charge-sheet is collusive, it can record that charge-sheet cannot be accepted and call upon the parties at any stage to adduce oral evidence of accident and alleged negligence.
In such cases, issue of negligence must be decided on other evidence ignoring the charge-sheet.
In the case of Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Cmpany Ltd vs Smt. Kamlesh and Others2009 (3) AD Delhi 310 it was held that an adverse inference can be drawn when the driver of the offending vehicle does not enter into the witness box.
The compensation should not be a windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.
17. The case of Raj Kumar vs Ajay Kumar & Another (2011) 1 SCC 343, is one of the most prominent judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court which deals with compensation in injuries cases.
Where the claimant suffers a permanent disability as a result of injuries, the assessment of compensation is also to be done under the head of loss of future earnings which would depend the effect and impact of such permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured.
The tribunal should not mechanically apply the percentage of permanent disability as the percentage of economic loss or loss of earning capacity.
What requires to be assessed by the tribunal is the effect of the permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured after assessing the loss of earning capacity in terms of percentage of the income.
It has to be quantified in terms of money to arrive at the future loss of earnings by applying standard multiplier method.
All injuries or permanent disabilities arising from injuries do not result in loss of earning capacity.
If there is no loss of employment or earning capacity, there may not be any need to award any compensation under the head of loss of future earnings, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities in consequent to his injuries.
For claiming compensation, necessity of employing a professional attendant/ care taker is not required and the petitioner should be compensated for the value of services of the family members,
which has been or would be necessitated by the wrong doing of the driver.
(DTC & Ors Vs. Lalita,
1983 ACJ 253).
Therefore, the petitioner is awarded a sum of Rs.10,000/- as attendant charges.
Apart from his oral assertion, petitioner has not produced any document to show that he was running any sort of business from anywhere.
No bill book, tax invoice etc have been placed or proved on record to show that petitioner was self-employed and doing any business.
Petitioner has not led any evidence to show what exact work he was doing prior to accident and for how many hours, to arrive at any conclusion that petitioner is not able to work as before, to his detriment and that it is due to accident solely.
Hence, petitioner is not entitled to any compensation under this head.
29. There is no evidence led by the petitioner to suggest that the longevity of petitioner has been adversely affected due to the accident in question and there is absoulutely no evidence to show any loss of expectation of life and thus, no sum of money as compensation is awarded towards Loss of expectation of life.
30.
As insurance company has contractual and statutory liability to indemnify the insured, the Insurance company is liable to compensate the third party.
However, the breach in question is not such as would affect the right of third party, once it is established that vehicle was covered under the policy of insurance.
Law is well settled that insurance company would be entitled for recovery of the compensation amount from the driver and registered owner /insured of the offending vehicle.
In case titled as Gurmeet Singh vs. The New India Assurance Co. Ltd & Ors, MAC App 288/2021 decided on 06.10.2023, it has been held that the respondent no. 3 / insure is entitled to recover the compensation amount paid to the claimants.
